section_texts.preamble: IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON GEOSCIENCE AND REMOTE SENSING, VOL. 63, 2025 Dual-Branch Convolution–Transformer Network With Spectral–Spatial Attention for Hyperspectral Image Classification Yao Lu , Yongshan Zhang , Senior Member, IEEE, Xinwei Jiang , Xiaobo Liu , Senior Member, IEEE, and Zhihua Cai Abstract— Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification is a key task in the field of remote sensing, aiming to assign category labels to each pixel by leveraging the spectral and spatial information in HSIs. Recently, many deep learning (DL) methods, such as con- volutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformers, have been applied to this task, achieving significant results. However, most existing patch-based DL methods often overlook the potential relationships between the central pixel and its surrounding pixels. Additionally, the unique spectral characteristics of HSIs, such as the high correlation between adjacent spectral bands and low dependence between distant bands, also require special attention. Based on this, we propose a novel dual-branch convolution– transformer network with spectral–spatial attention (CTSSA), which can effectively aggregate both local and global spectral– spatial features. Specifically, CTSSA comprises two core modules: the pyramid spectral attention module (PSAM) and the center transformer encoder (CenterTE). The former extracts highly discriminative spectral features through a hierarchical multiscale attention mechanism, capturing subtle differences between adja- cent spectral bands. The latter improves the original transformer encoder (TE) by introducing a center-attention mechanism to model the global relationship between the central pixel and its surrounding pixels, thereby enhancing classification accuracy while reducing computational complexity. Experimental results on four public datasets (Salinas, Pavia University, Houston, and WHUHi-LongKou) demonstrate that, compared with nine other networks, CTSSA achieves satisfactory performance with fewer parameters and relatively high efficiency. Index Terms— Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), hyper- spectral image (HSI) classification, pyramid spectral attention, transformer. Zhihua Cai is with the School of Computer Science, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan 430074, China, and also with the School of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Wuhan University of Engineering Science, Wuhan 430200, China (e-mail: zhcai@cug.edu.cn). INTRODUCTION YPERSPECTRAL images (HSIs) contain hundreds of contiguous spectral bands, spanning the visible to the infrared regions of the spectrum. These bands record detailed spectral features, enabling high-precision identification and distinction of objects. Due to its rich spectral and spatial information, HSI has found widespread applications in various fields in recent years, such as geological mapping [1], [2], [3], environmental monitoring [4], [5], mineral exploration [6], precision agriculture [7], and military reconnaissance [8]. A critical task in hyperspectral image analysis is classi- fication, which involves assigning a unique category label to each pixel. Traditional hyperspectral image classification methods mainly rely on handcrafted feature extraction and conventional machine learning algorithms, such as support vector machines (SVMs) [9], [10], k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) [11], morphological profiles (MPs) [12], sparse representation (SR) [13], and low-rank models [14]. However, these methods often struggle to capture the high-level abstract features of HSIs, resulting in suboptimal classification accuracy [15]. In recent years, deep learning (DL) methods have been extensively applied to HSI classification due to their ability to automatically learn complex feature representations from data. Various DL-based methods have been successfully employed for HSI classification [16], [17], [18], including generative adversarial networks (GANs) [19], recurrent neural networks (RNNs) [20], [21], stacked autoencoders (SAEs) [22], deep belief networks (DBNs) [23], [24], graph convolutional net- works (GCNs) [25], [26], [27], and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Among these architectures, CNNs have emerged as the dominant DL method for HSI classification due to their powerful ability to model local features [28], [29], [30]. Hu et al. [31] were the first to propose stacking multiple 1-D convolutional layers to extract deep spectral features for HSI classification. To further learn spatial information, Zhao and Du [32] proposed a spatial-based 2-D CNN to extract spatial and spectral features of the principal components. With the introduction of 3-D CNN by Hamida et al. [28] for HSI classification, the model became capable of better integrating the 3-D structural information of images. Roy et al. [33] combined the strengths of 3-D CNN and 2-D CNN to propose a hybrid CNN (HybridSN) model for HSI clas- 1558-0644 © 2025 IEEE. Zhong et al. [34] integrated 3-D CNN with residual blocks to design an end-to-end spectral–spatial residual network (SSRN), continuously learning discriminative features from spectral and spatial information while using batch normaliza- tion (BN) to enhance model performance. Zhou et al. [35] combined 3-D CNN with a feature pyramid structure to design a spectral–spatial pyramid network (SSPN), which uses the fusion of 3-D convolutions and multiscale convolutions to extract comprehensive spatial-spectral features. Although 3-D convolutional kernels reduce the parameter requirements compared to 2-D convolutions, methods based on 3-D CNN still involve a substantial number of parameters. Cui et al. [36] recently proposed LiteDepthwiseNet, which decomposes stan- dard convolutions into depthwise and pointwise convolutions, significantly reducing parameters while maintaining high clas- sification performance. Although CNNs dominate the field of computer vision due to their strong local feature extraction capabilities, they struggle to capture the global features or long-range dependencies in HSIs due to the limited receptive field of convolutional kernels. Recently, transformer networks based on the multihead self-attention (MHSA) mechanism have achieved significant success in the field of natural language processing (NLP). Dosovitskiy et al. [37] were the first to demonstrate the potential of vision transformer (ViT) for image classifica- tion tasks, achieving better performance than CNNs. ViT segments the input image into fixed-size patches (16 × 16) and treats each patch as a sequence input to the transformer encoder (TE), thereby capturing global features and generating high-level representations. Due to its capability to model long- range dependencies, Transformer networks have also been applied to HSI [38], [39], [40]. However, transformer-based approaches often overlook the details of local features [41] and are associated with a large number of parameters and increased training complexity [42], [43]. Relying solely on the transformer architecture makes it challenging to achieve satisfactory results. Therefore, some researchers have introduced the integra- tion of CNN and transformers to efficiently extract both local and global dependencies [44]. Sun et al. [45] proposed a spectral–spatial feature tokenization transformer (SSFTT) that effectively extracts local features using a hybrid CNN, transforms them into high-level semantic features using Gaussian-weighted tokenization, and captures deep relation- ships through a TE. Zhang et al. [46] developed a convolution transformer mixer (CTMixer), which integrates the advantages of ViT and CNN, utilizing a local-global MHSA mechanism to enhance classification accuracy. Li et al. [51] introduced HybridFormer, which uses a multigranularity token genera- tor to embed semantic tokens and replaces the traditional MHSA with a spatial-spectral attention (SSA) mechanism, effectively capturing global spatial and spectral dependencies in hyperspectral images. Yang et al. [47] proposed HiT, which embeds convolutional operations within the TE to extract spectral features and local spatial details. Xu et al. [48] proposed a double branch convolution–transformer network (DBCTNet) that combines a 3-D CNN with a convolution- enhanced TE. Through multiscale spectral feature extraction and a dual-branch structure, it effectively captures both local and global spatial and spectral information in hyperspectral images, significantly improving classification accuracy while reducing computational complexity. The aforementioned HSI classification methods each have their own characteristics. However, based on the char- acteristics of HSI, there is still room for further opti- mization and improvement, which can be summarized as follows. 1) Currently, most models extract spectral features from HSI in a relatively simplistic manner, without paying attention to the subtle differences between adjacent spectral bands, resulting in insufficient feature extrac- tion. Additionally, many attention-based models tend to process all spectral bands at once to extract globally representative features, which overlooks the distribution characteristics of spectral data. Specifically, adjacent spectral bands usually have high correlations, while the correlation between distant spectral bands is lower. At the same time, the spectral reflectance characteristics of different bands may be highly sensitive to the classi- fication of different materials. Although global attention mechanisms allow for the comprehensive learning of global significant features, some important local sig- nificant features may be diminished. This can lead to the loss of crucial discriminative information when the model fails to adequately focus on local features during classification. 2) In HSI classification, the patch-based methods typically extract a patch centered on each pixel as an input to the model, with the objective of predicting the class label of the center pixel. Since adjacent pixels contribute unequally to the classification of the center pixel, it is crucial to explore the potential correlations between the center pixel and its neighbors from a global perspective. As shown in Fig. 1, most existing mainstream HSI classification methods, whether based on CNNs or trans- formers, have overlooked the distinct importance of the center pixel in this task. CNNs generally assume that all pixels within the patch contribute equally to the center pixel’s classification, while transformers encode interac- tions uniformly among all pixels (i.e., queries, keys, and values), without considering their semantic relevance to the center pixel. However, in practical scenarios, only the pixels that are spatially and semantically related to the center pixel should exert significant influence on its classification, while heterogeneous pixels, such as those in noisy regions or along class boundaries, should be appropriately downweighted. This limitation becomes especially critical when classifying edge pix- els or regions with complex spatial layouts, where the absence of differentiated weighting in patch-based frameworks makes the model more susceptible to inter- ference from neighboring pixels of other categories, ultimately degrading classification accuracy. While this can improve the model’s performance to some extent, it does not fully harness the potential of CNNs in enhancing transformers. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel dual- branch convolution–transformer network with spectral–spatial attention (CTSSA). CTSSA integrates the strengths of convo- lutional networks and transformer architectures to effectively capture both local details and global contextual features. Specifically, we design a pyramid spectral attention module (PSAM) that employs a multiscale hierarchical grouping strat- egy combined with dynamic attention to adaptively extract both global and local spectral features. In addition, we intro- duce a center transformer encoder (CenterTE), specifically optimized for HSI classification, which explicitly models the global relationships between the center pixel and its sur- rounding neighbors using a center-guided sparse attention mechanism, while also reducing computational complexity. To compensate for the limitations of the CenterTE branch in capturing fine spatial-spectral details, we further design a dedicated 3D-CNN branch, enabling effective fusion of global contextual information and localized fine-grained features. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows. 1) To enhance the network’s capacity for extracting rich spectral information, we propose a novel PSAM. Unlike conventional approaches that process all spectral bands in a single pass, PSAM constructs a hierarchical grouped spectral feature processing framework, which leverages dynamic attention mechanisms to adaptively capture both global and local spectral features at multiple scales. This design ensures the diversity and effectiveness of the learned spectral representations. 2) To meet the specific demands of HSI classification, we design a new center-guided TE. This module utilizes a parameter-free center attention module (CAM) as the token mixer to selectively capture global contextual dependencies centered on the target pixel. Additionally, a convolutional multilayer perceptron (ConvMLP) is introduced as a channelwise MLP to further enhance local feature aggregation. This architecture significantly reduces model complexity while improving the model’s ability to selectively attend to relevant neighborhood information around the center pixel and suppress back- ground noise and class interference. 3) The proposed CTSSA
section_texts.method: integrates convolu- tional and transformer architectures through a dual- branch design. The CNN branch focuses on capturing fine-grained local spatial-spectral details, while the transformer branch is responsible for modeling global spatial context. This complementary design significantly improves the robustness and accuracy of hyperspectral image classification. The remainder of this article is structured as follows. Section II provides a detailed introduction to the proposed method, followed by a more in-depth description of the PSAM and CenterTE modules. In Section III, we present and analyze the experimental results. Finally, Section IV concludes our work. II. PROPOSED NETWORK We propose a novel dual-branch convolution–transformer network, termed CTSSA, specifically designed to address the unique challenges HSI classification through spectral–spatial attention mechanism. As illustrated in Fig. 2, CTSSA comprises three core components: 1) a PSAM, which extracts multiscale discriminative spectral features via a hierarchical structure; 2) a CenterTE, which explicitly enhances the role of the center pixel using a center-guided sparse attention mechanism, enabling effective modeling of global dependencies; and 3) a parallel 3D-CNN branch, responsible for capturing fine-grained local spectral–spatial features. This dual-branch architecture achieves complemen- tary feature learning, where the CenterTE branch focuses on global context, while the CNN branch preserves local detail, and ultimately performs feature fusion through an efficient cross-branch interaction mechanism. While maintain- ing a lightweight design with significantly fewer parameters, CTSSA consistently outperforms conventional methods in classification performance. A. PSAM Module HSIs typically contain hundreds of contiguous spectral bands, with each band capturing specific spectral informa- tion of materials within a scene [49]. These bands encode abundant compositional information but exhibit highly nonuni- form interband correlations, with strong correlations typically occurring between adjacent bands, while distant bands are often only weakly correlated. Moreover, the discriminative spectral characteristics of different land-cover categories may span various spectral scales. For instance, some classes rely on fine-grained narrowband features, such as the absorption peaks of minerals, whereas others require coarse-grained broadband features, like the overall low-reflectance profile of water bod- ies. Existing mainstream spectral feature extraction methods, including transformer-based global self-attention mechanisms and fixed-scale CNN architectures, are limited in effectively modeling such nonuniform correlations. Specifically, global self-attention treats all band relations equally, which not only leads to high computational overhead but also risks over- whelming subtle local features. On the other hand, convolution operations with fixed spectral groupings fail to adapt to Authorized licensed use limited to: CHONGQING UNIVERSITY. Although some recent methods have attempted spectral grouping, they typically adopt a single grouping scale, which may be insuf- ficient to capture multi-scale characteristics across categories. Furthermore, such approaches often lack the ability to model cross-group spectral relationships, leaving the extracted local features vulnerable to noise and prone to overfitting. To address these challenges, we propose a PSAM, whose core innovation lies in constructing a multilevel grouped spec- tral feature processing framework. By introducing a tunable hierarchical parameter H, PSAM enables multiresolution spec- tral analysis from global to local scales, allowing the model to capture discriminative features at varying granularities. As an illustrative example, we adopt a four-level pyramid configuration with H = {1, 2, 3, 6}, which is empirically validated as the optimal setting in subsequent ablation studies. HSI data can be represented as a 3-D tensor Rh×w×b, where h and w denote the spatial height and width of the image, respectively, and b represents the number of spectral bands. For each pixel, a 3-D local data cube X ∈Rp×p×b centered on that pixel is extracted, where p denotes the spatial patch size. This local cube is used as the input to the PSAM module, as shown in Fig. 2. After being input to the ith layer, X is divided along the spectral dimension into n subgroups, denoted as {X1 i , X2 i , . . . , Xn i }. The first level treats all spectral bands as a single group and employs global attention to capture the complete spectral curve structure. The second, third, and fourth levels divide the bands evenly into two, three, and six, groups, respectively. This hierarchical design enables the network to simultaneously model spectral correlations across different scales. Coarse-scale grouping is more robust to noise and better suited for capturing stable trends, whereas fine-scale grouping is capable of detecting subtle spectral variations. Within each subgroup, we design lightweight spectral attention block (SAB), as shown in Fig. 3, to dynamically compute the importance weights of spectral bands, thereby identifying informative bands and suppressing noise and redundancy. Fig. 3. Architecture of the proposed SAB module. In the implementation, for each spectral subgroup Xn i , the Key K and Value V representations are obtained via 1 × 1 convolutional kernels WK and WV , respectively, i.e., K n = WK ∗Xn and V n = WV ∗Xn i . This use of 1 × 1 convolution preserves the spatial locality of the feature maps while enabling efficient cross-band feature interaction. Notably, the Query Q is directly assigned as the original input, i = Xn i , thereby avoiding potential information loss intro- duced by feature transformations. This design ensures that the attention mechanism operates on the original observed spectral signals, allowing for more accurate band discrimination and preserving complete spectral information for the subsequent dual-branch architecture. Each Ei (i = 1, . . . , 4) represents the spectral features extracted at a different scale. B. CenterTE Branch Existing transformer-based methods for HSI classification, such as ViT and SpectralFormer, have demonstrated strong capabilities in modeling global dependencies. However, these approaches do not explicitly account for the unique role of the center pixel during attention computation. Moreover, traditional self-attention mechanisms incur high computational complexity and are prone to incorporating redundant informa- tion, such as background noise. In addition, in current hybrid transformer-CNN architectures, the transformer branch still relies on standard MHSA, which has not been specifically optimized for the characteristics of HSI classification tasks. To address the aforementioned issues, we design a novel TE tailored for HSI classification, named CenterTE. In this architecture, a CAM is introduced to replace the standard MHSA, enabling center-guided sparse attention. Additionally, a ConvMLP is employed to enhance local feature aggregation, compensating for potential detail loss due to the global nature of CAM. CNN Branch To compensate for the limitations of the CenterTE branch in capturing fine-grained local spatial-spectral details, we further design a dedicated 3D-CNN branch. Specifically, the CenterTE branch, guided by the center attention mechanism, primarily focuses on modeling global contextual dependencies, making it well-suited for perceiving and reasoning over the entire image region. However, it may underrepresent subtle spectral variations, textural patterns, and detailed structures present in localized regions. To address this issue, the 3D-CNN branch is introduced to leverage the high sensitivity of 3-D convolutions across both spatial and spectral dimensions, along with their strong capability in local feature extraction. This enables the precise modeling of localized spatial structures and spectral variations, providing critical support in scenes with blurred boundaries, intricate class interleaving, and rich local details. The inherent complementarity between the local (3D-CNN) and global (CenterTE) branches, in terms of scale and dimensional focus, is the fundamental motivation for integrating the 3D-CNN branch. By fusing the outputs of both branches, the network achieves effective coordination between local detail and global context, thereby significantly enhancing the performance of hyperspectral image classification. As illustrated in Fig. 2, the structure of this branch is straightforward and efficient. It consists of a Conv3D layer with a kernel size of 1 × 1 × 7, a depthwise 3-D convo- lution (DWConv3D) layers with kernel sizes of 3 × 3 × 3, an additional Conv3D layer, and residual connections. This combination of depthwise and standard convolutions allows for more effective extraction of local spatial-spectral features. Specifically, the multiscale spectral features YPSAM produced by the PSAM module are first passed through a 16-channel Conv3D layer for channel adjustment and spectral dimension- ality reduction. Then, grouped convolutions via DWConv3D layers are applied to extract refined local features across both spatial and spectral domains. Finally, another Conv3D layer integrates the localized spatial-spectral information to produce the final output of this branch. Residual connections are incorporated within the branch to alleviate gradient vanishing and improve training stability. The process can be formulated Ycnn = Conv3D1×1×7(YPSAM) Zcnn = Conv3D(DWConv3D(Ycnn)) ⊕Ycnn. (11) The outputs from the center TE branch and the 3D-CNN branch are concatenated along the channel dimension, fol- lowed by a Conv3D layer with a kernel size of 1 × 1 × 1 to perform feature fusion. Finally, global average pooling (GAP) is applied to flatten the fused feature map into a vector, which is then passed through a fully connected layer to produce the final classification result. After concatenation along the channel dimension, these features are further fused via a pointwise convolution, resulting in a final feature map with dimensions (16, p × p × 1). In the classification stage, GAP flattens the fused feature map into a feature vector of size (16×1), which is then mapped to target categories through a fully connected layer, producing a final output of dimension (d × 1), where d corresponds to the number of classification categories. III. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS In this section, we conduct experiments on four public HSI datasets to validate the effectiveness of the proposed CTSSA. Nine DL models were selected for comparison, including three models purely based on CNN (SSRN [34], FDSSC [50], and DBDA [51]), two models based on trans- formers (SpectralFormer [52] and morphFormer [53]), and four models combining CNN and transformer architectures (SSFTT [45], GSC-ViT [54], DCTN [55], and DBCTNet [48]). Three quantitative metrics [overall accuracy (OA), average accuracy (AA), and kappa coefficient] were employed to evaluate the performance of each method. Experimental Setup First, the experiments were conducted on a machine equipped with an NVIDIA GTX 1660Ti GPU, utilizing the PyTorch [56] DL framework. Second, focal loss [57] was used during the network training, a method that has been proven to be effective in HSI classification, especially for addressing class imbalance issues [58], [59]. The formula for focal loss is as follows: Lfocal = −αy �1 −py γ log �py (12) where y is the true class, py is the predicted probability of class y, and αy and γ are the tunable hyperparameters. Specifically, αy adjusts class weights to reduce bias, while γ focuses learning on hard samples. For the SA, PU, HS, and LK datasets, γ was set to 4.2, 0.5, 1.9, and 5.0, respectively, and α was set as the inverse of each class’s sample proportion. Finally, in the experiments, Adam was used as the optimizer, and the warmup strategy from [48] was referenced to ensure stable convergence of the model. The warmup strategy follows the following formula: lr(t) = 2 × η × 1 + cos π × t −ω T −ω if t ∈(ω, T ] η × max 0, t if t ∈[0, ω] otherwise (13) where η represents the preset maximum learning rate, t is the current training step, T is the total number of training steps, and ω is the number of warmup steps. The learning rate gradually increases from zero to the maximum value of η and then decreases back to zero. In the experiments, the warmup steps accounted for one-tenth of the total training steps. The learning rates for the SA, PU, HS, and LK datasets were set to 0.001, 0.001, 0.003, and 0.001, respectively. The weight decay for Adam was set to 0.001. All models were trained for 400, 400, 600, and 400 epochs on the SA, PU, HS, and LK datasets, respectively, with patch sizes of 13 × 13, 13 × 13, 15 × 15, and 9 × 9. The batch size was set to 128, and the number of hierarchical scales H = {1, 2, 3, 6}. C. CONCLUSION In this article, we propose a novel dual-branch convolution– transformer method based on spectral-SA, named CTSSA, for HSI classification. CTSSA effectively addresses the limitations of the existing models in spectral detail extraction and center pixel attention by integrating a PSAM module and a CenterTE module. Unlike processing all spectral bands simultaneously, our proposed PSAM module employs a hierarchical, mul- tiscale attention mechanism to segment and group spectral information, selectively focusing on critical features across different bands. This approach allows for finer extraction of high-discriminative spectral details, particularly capturing subtle differences between adjacent spectral bands. Addition- ally, we designed a novel CenterTE module to model the global relationships between the central pixel and its surround- ing pixels, thereby improving classification accuracy while reducing computational complexity. We further introduced a 3-D CNN branch to effectively extract and integrate local spatial information into the network. Finally, we conducted comparative experiments against nine existing algorithms. The results demonstrate that the proposed CTSSA achieves superior performance on four public HSI datasets with fewer parameters and FLOPs. In future work, we aim to explore self-supervised and transfer learning approaches to enhance feature learning under limited sample conditions. Meanwhile, we will focus on optimizing the network structure, particularly improving the interaction mechanisms between the dual branches to promote deeper feature fusion, thereby boosting training efficiency and classification accuracy.

This dual-branch architecture achieves complemen- tary feature learning, where the CenterTE branch focuses on global context, while the CNN branch preserves local detail, and ultimately performs feature fusion through an efficient cross-branch interaction mechanism.

Existing mainstream spectral feature extraction methods, including transformer-based global self-attention mechanisms and fixed-scale CNN architectures, are limited in effectively modeling such nonuniform correlations.
Furthermore, such approaches often lack the ability to model cross-group spectral relationships, leaving the extracted local features vulnerable to noise and prone to overfitting.
